body:
I like this proposal. This will help with canvas use-cases (WebGL, 2D), in addition to the original motivation of allowing flicker-free image loading UX.

A couple of comments though:

## Image identity

I think the decoded size should only apply to the `const img = new Image()` object exclusively. The example seems to imply that the decoded size will apply to all images source from the same `src` value, i.e. globally to everything sourced from "4000x4000.jpg". That means the same image cannot be decoded at different sizes, which I think is an unnecessary limitation. Consider alternatives, such as cloning the decoded image element, object URLs, or a new method for transferring an image from one element to another (a la `transferFromImageBitmap`).

## Updating decoded size

Maybe this is implied in the proposal, but it would be nice to make it explicit. While the destination size may be known ahead of time, there's no guarantee that it won't change. So the same image may need to be resampled to something else. One way to do this is to allow calling `decode` multiple times, supplying different target dimensions.

## Stronger memory guarantees

After the image is decoded and transferred to, say, WebGL, the `Image` object may no longer be necessary. However, it's unclear when the underlying memory would be freed. Theoretically, setting the `src` value to "" would leave no strong references to the underlying image data, and browsers could reclaim memory eagerly. However, the spec doesn't seem to specify this. It would be nice to add it to the spec so developers could rely on it.
I'm going to copy @whatwg/canvas on this given the likely overlap of audiences and the lack of a similar group of people for images.

For the canvas uses wouldn't it better to use an ImageBitmap instead of ``. You can specify the resize size (and crop region) directly. Using it instead of `decode()` for DOM purposes seems hacky, but then again that use case seems more complex since the actual size can be a lot more dynamic with less control by the author over when things would update (e.g. the user moving the page to a monitor with a different pixel density).

Not sure `decode()` is the right API for this, as it opens question about reusing the same image URL in multiple places.
Also I'm not sure in general about having this as a JS only API.
I wonder if we could use fragment directives for this? e.g. `my-image.jpg#:~:size=100,100`
cc @eeeps

Firefox supports multiple different output surface sizes simultaneously from one img element (or from one image URL in different places). That seems like a reasonable model to use to solve the "same image cannot be decoded at different sizes" and "same image URL in multiple places" problem. Having a size provided in the decode() call would naturally fit into Firefox's current image rendering implementation. In fact it would help us avoid extra decodes in the situation that the image is drawn at a different size from the intrinsic size.

> Not sure `decode()` is the right API for this, as it opens question about reusing the same image URL in multiple places. Also I'm not sure in general about having this as a JS only API. I wonder if we could use fragment directives for this? e.g. `my-image.jpg#:~:size=100,100`

https://www.w3.org/TR/media-frags/#naming-space is of a certain vintage but exists, when dealing with URLs.
Can you just key the decode requests by element and requested size?

Assuming that #large-image is a different element and rendered at a different size, then yes that would decode twice. This is how Firefox works today. We can key off the entry in the list of available images (effectively the URL) and requested decode size.

OK I see. That makes sense, though I still wish this didn't *have* to depend on script. There are pure-HTML use cases for this I think. Perhaps it can be a boolean attribute on `` or some such to make it decode using the specified width/height?

> Not sure `decode()` is the right API for this, as it opens question about reusing the same image URL in multiple places. Also I'm not sure in general about having this as a JS only API. I wonder if we could use fragment directives for this? e.g. `my-image.jpg#:~:size=100,100`

I think `decode()` is a just hint from JS to the display engine saying: "I am going to use this image momentarily, so get it ready for display". My suggestion just tries to make this hint more specific. This way the image sub-sampling can be utilized to save memory and CPU. 

I am not sure about other browsers, but in WebKit there is no guarantee if you decode an image and then try to use it later, the decoded frame will be available. Under memory pressure, WebKit releases all the decoded frames, except some exceptions, to save the application from being jetsam. The image frame will be decoded whenever it is needed.

Setting the image src to the image URL is just a way to tell browser display engine to draw this frame now.

Using `my-image.jpg#:~:size=100,100` will make different URLs for different sizes which will be a memory regression.

> For the canvas uses wouldn't it better to use an ImageBitmap instead of ``. You can specify the resize size (and crop region) directly. Using it instead of `decode()` for DOM purposes seems hacky, but then again that use case seems more complex since the actual size can be a lot more dynamic with less control by the author over when things would update (e.g. the user moving the page to a monitor with a different pixel density). To get an image to be displayed on a canvas or on an ImageBitmap, the image has to be decoded. Decoding an image with its natural size can be very expensive. If you know that a large image will be displayed in a much smaller size, it is better to decode for this small size from the beginning. The image source can have multiple versions with different sizes and it will help you save memory and CPU if you decode for a certain smaller size.

Using it instead of `decode()` for DOM purposes seems hacky, but then again that use case seems more complex since the actual size can be a lot more dynamic with less control by the author over when things would update (e.g. the user moving the page to a monitor with a different pixel density). > > To get an image to be displayed on a canvas or on an ImageBitmap, the image has to be decoded. Decoding an image with its natural size can be very expensive. If you know that a large image will be displayed in a much smaller size, it is better to decode for this small size from the beginning. The image source can have multiple versions with different sizes and it will help you save memory and CPU if you decode for a certain smaller size. Yes, and `createImageBitmap` lets the author specify the source size, and the resize size, so the UA can use that info to decode using the best settings. So for canvas, authors should use an ImageBitmap rather than img + decode().

Developers who care enough to do a good job when given a new tool like this already have a way to help with memory pressure, with responsive images. The first question that comes to mind is: what use cases are there for this that wouldn't be better served by pre-rendering a different width and serving that (which would also help with bandwidth)? I can imagine a few -- displaying user uploads, or any other scenario where the person writing the markup isn't in control of the resources (toxic org silos, hotlinking...). How common are those? A much bigger benefit could be had by doing this sort of thing automatically. I suppose that could only work for lazy-loaded images, and would trigger multiple decodes if layout size expands after the initial decode, which could be problematic. But it would be neat if: ``` ``` Just decoded to a width of 150px * window.devicePixelRatio, without devs having to opt in to anything.
